youtube.description: In this episode you will explain that every variable has an address, use the address-of operator and tell an address from a value, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 Memory and addresses · 1:29 The gap between boxes · 2:38 Addresses in a row · 3:24 Second program · 4:43 Recap · 5:13 Bug of the Day · 6:13 Challenge · 6:35 Next episode

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today we look under the hood. Every variable lives at an address in memory. Soon you will use that address.

scenes.onScreen: "Memory and addresses": numbered lines (1. Memory is a long row of numbered bytes; 2. Every variable lives at an address; 3. The ampersand gives the address) and an analogy card: a street of houses: each house has a number, and a family inside
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: Memory is a long row of bytes. Each byte has a number, called its address. A variable lives at one address, and it fills as many bytes as its type needs. The ampersand in front of a variable gives its address. Think of a street of houses. Each house has a number, and a family lives inside. Why should a beginner care about addresses? Because the most powerful tools in C plus plus work with them. Pointers, arrays and the heap all depend on this idea. Addresses are long numbers, and we usually write them in a base that uses letters too. You do not need to read them. You only need to know that each variable has one, and that no two variables share the same bytes.
points: Memory is a long row of numbered bytes
Every variable lives at an address

scenes.onScreen: gap.cpp: the distance in bytes between two neighbouring ints
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 5] An array of three ints. [HL 6] The ampersand gives the address of the first item. We view it as a char address, so that we can count bytes. [HL 7] This is the address of the second item. [HL 8] The difference is four bytes. That is the size of one int. The real addresses change from run to run, but the gap is always four. [HL 5] Three ints sit side by side in memory. [HL 6] The ampersand gives the address of the first item. We turn it into a char pointer, so we can count in single bytes. [HL 7] The same trick gives the address of the second item. [HL 8] The difference is four. An int takes four bytes, so the next item starts four bytes later.

scenes.onScreen: three int boxes and their addresses, four bytes apart
scenes.animation: Boxes pop in one by one with size and address tags; arrows draw on as the narrator mentions them; regions are labelled; pop per box
scenes.narration: Look at the three boxes. The first sits at address one thousand. The next sits at one thousand and four. The last at one thousand and eight. These addresses are examples. On a real computer, the numbers differ every time you run the program. Notice that every box has an address, a size and a value. The address says where it starts. The size says where it ends. The value is what the bytes mean for that type.

scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 5] A char takes one byte. [HL 6] An int takes four. [HL 7] A double takes eight. [HL 8] An address itself takes eight bytes on a sixty-four-bit computer. Remember this. We will store addresses in variables soon. [HL 5] A char takes one byte. [HL 6] An int takes four bytes on most machines. [HL 7] A double takes eight. [HL 8] A pointer to an int is also a fixed size. On a modern computer with sixty-four bits, it takes eight bytes. Every pointer has the same size, whatever it points to.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as sizes dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. The program prints one, four, eight and eight on four lines. Notice that the size of a pointer does not depend on the type behind it. An int star and a double star are both eight.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. Memory is a long row of numbered bytes. Two. Every variable lives at an address. Three. The ampersand gives the address of a variable. Four. An address is not the same as a value. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: Memory is a long row of numbered bytes.
Every variable lives at an address.
The ampersand gives the address of a variable.
An address is not the same as a value.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: Storing an address in an int
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the g++ error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We store the address of fish in a plain int. The compiler says invalid conversion from int star to int. An address has its own type. For the address of an int, that type is int star. We learn it in the next episode. An address is not a number that you can store in an int. It has its own type, and the type remembers what lives at that address. The compiler stops the mistake, and that is good. Store the address in a pointer.

bug.error:
Compiler output (exactly as g++ prints it):

addr.cpp: In function 'int main()':
addr.cpp:6:17: error: invalid conversion from 'int*' to 'int' [-fpermissive]
    6 |     int where = &fish;
      |                 ^~~~~
      |                 |
      |                 int*
bug.why: An address has its own type. For an int, the type is int star. A plain int cannot hold it.

pun: "My variable moved house. It left a new address, but it forgot to tell its neighbours."
challenge: Make an array of two doubles. Print the number of bytes between the two items. Hint: a double takes eight bytes, so the answer should be eight.
challengeAnswer: Take the address of each item, convert both to char star, and subtract. The answer is eight.
